sections.normalized_html:
A chi-square random variable [MATH: X \sim \chi^2(k)] with [MATH: k] degrees of freedom has the following probability density function:

[MATH: {(1)/(2^{k/2}Γ((k)/(2)))x^{k/2 − 1}e^{− x/2},|x ≥ 0; 0,|otherwise]

We're given that [MATH: X\sim \chi^2(4).] So, [MATH: X] has the following probability density function:

[MATH: {(1)/(4Γ(2))xe^{− x/2},|x ≥ 0; 0,|otherwise]

Recalling that [MATH: \Gamma(n) = (n-1)!] for any natural number [MATH: n \geq 1,] we have

[MATH: \Gamma(2) = 1! = 1.]

So, the probability distribution becomes

[MATH: {(1)/(4)xe^{− x/2},|x ≥ 0; 0,|otherwise.]

Finally, we calculate [MATH: P\left(X < 5\right)] as follows:

[MATH: P(X < 5)|= ∫_{0}^{5}f(x)dx; = ∫_{0}^{5}(1)/(4)xe^{− x/2}dx; = (1)/(4)∫_{0}^{5}xe^{− x/2}dx; ≈ (1)/(4) ⋅ 2.85081; ≈ 0.7127]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The chi-square distribution with [MATH: k] degrees of freedom, denoted [MATH: \chi^2(k)], is the distribution of a random variable that is the sum of the squares of [MATH: k] independent standard normal random variables.

Content:
Thus, if [MATH: Z_1, Z_2, \ldots, Z_k] are mutually independent, where [MATH: Z_i\sim N(0,1)], then
[MATH: Z_1^2+Z_2^2+\ldots+Z_k^2\sim \chi^2(k).]

Content:
It can be shown that [MATH: X \sim \chi^2(k)] has the following probability density function:

Content:
[MATH: {(1)/(2^{k/2}Γ((k)/(2)))x^{k/2 − 1}e^{− x/2},|x ≥ 0; 0,|otherwise]

EXPLANATION
